'''Emily Riehl''' is an American [[mathematician]] who has contributed to [[higher category theory]] and [[homotopy theory]]. Much of her work, including her PhD thesis,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Riehl|first=Emily|date=2011|title=Algebraic model structures|url=http://emis.de/journals/NYJM/j/2011/17-10v.pdf|journal=[[The New York Journal of Mathematics]]|volume=17|pages=173–231|mr=2781914|archive-date=2022-01-27|access-date=2022-04-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220127101146/http://www.emis.de/journals/NYJM/j/2011/17-10v.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> concerns [[Model category|model structures]] and more recently the foundations of [[infinity-categories]].<ref name=phdplus>{{Cite web|url=https://blogs.ams.org/phdplus/2017/08/19/category-theory-and-context-an-interview-with-emily-riehl/|title=Category Theory and Context: An Interview with Emily Riehl|last=Malmskog|first=Beth|date=August 19, 2017|website=AMS Blogs|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180308161456/https://blogs.ams.org/phdplus/2017/08/19/category-theory-and-context-an-interview-with-emily-riehl/|archive-date=March 8, 2018|url-status=live|access-date=March 8, 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sciencefriday.com/articles/women-taking-math-next-dimension/ |title=The Women Taking Math To The Next Dimension |last=Young |first=Lauren J. |website=[[Science Friday]] |date=2017-11-17 |access-date=2018-03-08}}</ref> She is the author of two textbooks<ref name="AMS">{{Cite journal|last1=Readdy|first1=Margaret|last2=Taylor|first2=Christine|date=March 2018|title=Women's History Month|journal=[[Notices of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=65|issue=3|pages=248–303|doi=10.1090/noti1653|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="baez">{{cite web|url=http://math.ucr.edu/home/baez/books.html |title=How to Learn Math and Physics |first=John C. |last=Baez |author-link=John C. Baez |website=[[University of California, Riverside]] |access-date=2018-03-08 |date=2016-01-02}}</ref> and serves on the editorial boards of three journals.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.springer.com/mathematics/geometry/journal/40062/PS2?detailsPage=editorialBoard |title=Editorial board |website=Journal of Homotopy and Related Structures |publisher=[[Springer Science+Business Media|Springer]] |access-date=2018-03-08 |archive-date=2018-03-09 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180309054529/https://www.springer.com/mathematics/geometry/journal/40062/PS2?detailsPage=editorialBoard |url-status=dead }}<br />{{cite web |url=http://intlpress.com/site/pub/pages/journals/items/hha/_home/editorial/index.html |title=Editorial board |website=[[Homology, Homotopy and Applications]] |access-date=2018-03-08 }}<br />{{cite web |url=http://cahierstgdc.com/index.php/editorial-board/ |title=Editorial Board |website=[[Cahiers de Topologie et Géométrie Différentielle Catégoriques]] |access-date=2018-03-08 }}</ref>

== Education and career ==
Riehl was born in [[Thousand Oaks, California]] and grew up in [[Bloomington-Normal, Illinois]].<ref name="s529">{{cite web | last=Keiger | first=Dale | title=The mathematic mind of Emily Riehl | website=The Hub | date=2021-12-13 | url=https://hub.jhu.edu/magazine/2021/winter/emily-riehl-category-theory/ }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Perkins|first=S.|date=16 March 2002|title=Science Smarts|journal=Science News|volume=161|issue=11|pages=165–166|doi=10.2307/4013075|jstor=4013075}}</ref>
As a high school student at [[University High School (Normal, Illinois)|University High School]] in Normal in 2002, she won third place in the national [[Intel Science Talent Search]] for a project in mathematics entitled "On the Properties of Tits Graphs".<ref>{{cite web|title=Students Awarded $530,000 At Intel Science Talent Search|publisher=Intel|url=https://www.intel.com/pressroom/archive/releases/2002/20020311corp_a.htm|date=March 11, 2002|access-date=March 8, 2018}}</ref>

Riehl attended [[Harvard University]] as an undergraduate; with [[Benedict Gross]] as a mentor, she wrote a senior thesis on [[local class field theory]]. She also headed the school [[Rugby football|rugby]] team (in which she played as a [[Rugby union positions#Scrum-half|scrum-half]]) and played viola in the Harvard–Radcliffe Orchestra.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Harvard Magazine|department=Stellar Seniors|url=https://harvardmagazine.com/2006/05/stellar-seniors-html|title=Emily Riehl|first=Elizabeth S.|last=Widdicombe|date=May–June 2006}}</ref> After Harvard, she completed [[Part III of the Mathematical Tripos|part III of the Maths Tripos at Cambridge]].<ref name="AMS" /> She defended her doctoral dissertation, ''Algebraic model structures'', at the [[University of Chicago]] in 2011, supervised by [[J. Peter May]].<ref>{{MathGenealogy|id=153426}}</ref>

Between 2011 and 2015, Riehl held a position at Harvard University as a Benjamin Peirce Postdoctoral Fellow. Since 2015, she has been employed at [[Johns Hopkins University]], where she became an [[associate professor]] in 2019.  She became a full professor in 2022, and was appointed to JHU's [[Kelly Miller (scientist)|Kelly Miller]] professorship of mathematics in July 2024.<ref>{{cite web | title=CV | url=https://emilyriehl.github.io/cv/ }}</ref>

In addition, she teaches on [[edX]] and has hosted videos for [[Numberphile]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://online-learning.harvard.edu/author/emily-riehl |title=Emily Riehl, Harvard Online Learning Portal |website=[[Harvard University]] |date=28 February 2018 |access-date=2018-03-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.numberphile.com/team/|title=Numberphile – Videos about Numbers and Stuff|website=Numberphile|access-date=2018-03-08|archive-date=2018-07-15|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180715065744/http://numberphile.com/team/|url-status=dead}}<br />{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qcv1IqHWAzg|title=Stable Marriage Problem – Numberphile|website=[[YouTube]]|date=2014-09-04|access-date=2018-03-08}}</ref> Along with Benedict Gross and Joe Harris, she developed a Harvard course on edX titled "Fat Chance: Probability from the Ground Up".<ref>{{Cite web|title=Fat Chance: Probability from the Ground Up|url=https://www.edx.org/course/fat-chance-probability-from-the-ground-up-2|access-date=2020-07-29|website=edX|language=en}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
In January 2020, Riehl received the JHU President's Frontier Award, a $250,000 award that "supports individuals at Johns Hopkins who are breaking new ground and poised to become leaders in their field".  She is the sixth JHU faculty member to receive the award.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://hub.jhu.edu/2020/01/16/emily-riehl-mathematics-frontier-award-999-em1-art1-dtd-news/|title=Mathematician Emily Riehl earns President's Frontier Award|date=January 16, 2020|author=Sandy Alexander|publisher=Hub –Johns Hopkins University}}</ref>

Riehl was awarded the 2021 AWM [[Joan & Joseph Birman Research Prize in Topology and Geometry|Joan & Joseph Birman Research Prize]] "for her deep and foundational work in category theory and homotopy theory."<ref>{{Cite web|title=AWM Joan & Joseph Birman Research Prizes|url=https://awm-math.org/awards/awm-birman-research-prize/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Joan and Joseph Birman Research Prize 2021|url=https://awm-math.org/awards/awm-birman-research-prize/birman-research-prize-2021/}}</ref> She is the fourth winner of this prize. She was named a Fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]], in the 2022 class of fellows, "for contributions to research, exposition, and communication in higher category theory".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/cgi-bin/fellows/fellows_by_year.cgi|title=2022 Class of Fellows of the AMS|publisher=American Mathematical Society|access-date=2021-11-05}}</ref> In 2022 she was awarded a [[Simons Foundation|Simons]] Fellowship,<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-18 |title=2022 Simons Fellows in Mathematics and Theoretical Physics Announced |url=https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2022/02/18/2022-simons-fellows-in-mathematics-and-theoretical-physics-announced/ |access-date=2022-07-04 |website=Simons Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref> and again in 2026.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-02-18 |title=2026 Simons Fellows in Mathematics Announced |url= https://www.simonsfoundation.org/2026/04/10/2026-simons-fellows-in-mathematics-announced/ |access-date=2026-08-29|website=Simons Foundation |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Service and outreach ==

Riehl is a host of the n-Category Café, a blog on subjects related to category theory in mathematics, physics, and philosophy.<ref>{{cite web |title=The n-Category Café |url=https://golem.ph.utexas.edu/category/ |access-date=7 October 2019}}</ref> She was a board member of the LGBT mathematical association [[Spectra (mathematical association)|Spectra]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Spectra: The Association for LGBT Mathematicians |url=http://lgbtmath.org/Board.html |access-date=20 August 2022}}</ref>

== Other activities ==
In addition to her mathematical work, Riehl has competed on the [[United States women's national Australian rules football team]] at the [[Australian Football International Cup]],<ref name=phdplus /><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.footyalmanac.com.au/footy-town-kick-like-a-girl-score-like-a-lady/|title=Footy Town: Kick like a girl, score like a lady|website=The Footy Almanac|last=Holt |first=Stephanie |date=2013-05-17|access-date=2018-03-08}}</ref> and was vice captain of the team at the 2017 cup.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://usafl.com/news/20170731/freedom-captains-ready-ic-challenge|title=Freedom Captains Ready for IC Challenge|first=Brian|last=Barrish|date=July 31, 2017|publisher=United States Australian Football League}}</ref>

She plays [[viola]], [[guitar]], and formerly played [[bass guitar]] in the band Unstraight.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.highclouds.org/interview-lgbt-movement-and-feminism-with-queer-band-unstraight/ |title=Interview: LGBT movement and feminism with queer band Unstraight|website=Highclouds|date=2017-02-15|access-date=2018-03-08}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://hub.jhu.edu/magazine/2021/winter/emily-riehl-category-theory/|title=The {{not a typo|mathematic}} mind of Emily Riehl|first=Dale|last=Keiger|date=Winter 2021|magazine=Johns Hopkins Magazine|access-date=2025-11-15}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202105/rnoti-p824.pdf|title=2021 AWM Annual Meeting Prizes|department=Mathematics People|pages=827–828|date=May 2021|volume=68|issue=5}}</ref>
